warmup.q: Pod A takes a lock with a 10-second lease, then stops for 15 seconds, for any of lesson 4's reasons. Meanwhile pod B takes the lock and writes the payout file. Which change stops A from overwriting B's file when it wakes up?
options: Release the lock with compare-and-delete instead of DEL
Move the lock from Redis to etcd, which replicates it with consensus
Make the file store refuse writes that carry an older fencing token
warmup.why: The pause happens after A got the lock, so nothing on the lock service's side can stop A from writing when it wakes: A doesn't know its lease ended. Compare-and-delete only stops A from deleting B's lock. etcd keeps the lock safe from a server crash, not from a holder that paused after taking it; Jepsen lost about 18% of the updates guarded by etcd 3.4.3 locks under pauses. A longer lease just needs a longer pause. Only the store sees both writes, so only the store can refuse the stale one, if each write carries a number that grows with every lock holder.

sections.h: A lease is a lock that runs out, and a Redis key can be one
sections.html:
Lesson 4 ended with holder A writing 1.4 seconds after its lease ran out, and a ledger that applied the write anyway. This lesson builds that lease into a real lock and then gives the resource a way to refuse the late write. Redis is the worked example, because a Redis lock is a single command you can watch. etcd and ZooKeeper come in where they differ.

The nightly settlement batch builds the payout file that tells the bank how much to pay each merchant. A scheduler in each of 3 pods starts it, because one scheduler would be a single point of failure. It must run once: if two pods build and send the file, merchants are paid twice.

Inside one JVM you would reach for synchronized or a ReentrantLock. Three pods share no memory, so the lock has to live somewhere they can all reach. The Caching track's lesson on how Redis executes commands gives you the first piece: one thread runs every command, so a command that creates a key only if it doesn't exist is a perfect "first one wins". SET lock:settle pod-a NX answers OK to exactly one pod and nil to the others. Holding the lock means the key exists, and releasing it is DEL.

That breaks the first time the holder dies. Pod A is OOM-killed halfway through the batch, the key stays forever, and no pod ever runs the batch again. So the lock needs a deadline: SET lock:settle pod-a NX PX 30000. The PX has to be inside the SET, for the same reason the Caching track's rate limiter needed one command: a crash between SETNX and EXPIRE leaves a key with no TTL. A lock with a deadline is a lease, the thing lesson 4's holders kept renewing.

The deadline is what makes the lock work, and what makes it dangerous. Redis deletes the key after 30 seconds whether or not the holder has finished, and nothing tells the holder. Suppose the batch runs slower than usual, or pod A stops for 35 seconds for any of lesson 4's reasons. The lease runs out. Pod B's SET NX succeeds and B starts the batch too. Then A finishes and runs DEL lock:settle, which deletes B's lock, not A's. Pod C's SET NX succeeds while B is still running. Three pods have run a batch that must run once, and every step looked correct from where it ran.

That is the model for this lesson, and it holds for every lock service, not just Redis. A lease is a record that says who may act, until a deadline. The lock service enforces the deadline. Nothing enforces that the holder stops acting when the deadline passes. Each of the next sections deals with one consequence of that.

try.title: Let a lease run out, then delete the wrong lock
steps: Open two redis-cli prompts from the labs folder (docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli), one for pod A and one for pod B. Start the server first if needed.
Pod A clears any lock left from an earlier run and takes the lock with a 10-second lease; pod B tries at once and checks the TTL. Then wait at least 10 seconds: A is "paused".
Pod B tries again. Then pod A, which knows nothing about the pause, releases with DEL. Finally a third pod tries. Predict every reply first.

code.title: two prompts (lines starting with # are notes)
code.html:
# pod A
DEL lock:settle
SET lock:settle pod-a NX PX 10000
# pod B
SET lock:settle pod-b NX PX 10000
PTTL lock:settle
# wait 10 seconds: A's lease runs out while A is "paused"
PTTL lock:settle
SET lock:settle pod-b NX PX 30000
# pod A wakes up and releases its lock
DEL lock:settle
# pod B (playing pod C)
SET lock:settle pod-c NX PX 30000
GET lock:settle

try.expect: The first DEL prints (integer) 0, or 1 if an earlier run left the key behind. A's SET prints OK and B's first SET prints (nil); PTTL shows just under 10000. After the wait, PTTL prints (integer) -2: the key is gone. B's SET prints OK, so B now holds the lock. A's DEL prints (integer) 1: it deleted B's lock, and A can't tell from the reply. Pod C's SET prints OK while B is still "working", and GET shows "pod-c".

sections.h: Release only your own lock, in one command
sections.html:
To stop A from deleting B's lock, each lock must say whose it is. Each acquire stores a random value that only that holder knows, a token: SET lock:settle 6f1e... NX PX 30000, with a fresh UUID every time. The Redis docs suggest 20 random bytes; a random UUID has 122 random bits, which is plenty. A pod name won't do, because the same pod can hold the lock twice in a row, and its old attempt and its new one would look identical.

The obvious release is GET the key, compare it with my token in Java, and DEL if they match. It is the check-then-act race from the Transactions track's lesson on Redis MULTI, WATCH and Lua. There is a gap between A's GET and A's DEL, and a pause can land in it: A reads its own token, a GC stops A, A's lease expires, B acquires, and A's DEL deletes B's lock after all. The simulator below lets you produce exactly that.

The compare and the delete have to be one command. The classic way is the Lua script from the Redis docs:

if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
    return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1])
end
return 0

It returns 1 when it deleted my lock, and 0 when the key holds someone else's token, or doesn't exist. Redis 8.4 made it a single built-in command: DELEX lock:settle IFEQ <token>, which is redis.delex(key, CompareCondition.valueEq(token)) in Jedis. Extending a lease needs the same care, because it must only push out my own deadline: SET lock:settle <token> IFEQ <token> PX 30000 on Redis 8.4, or a script that compares the token before PEXPIRE.

etcd's and ZooKeeper's lock recipes avoid this mistake by design: every waiting client creates its own key (in ZooKeeper, a sequential node), the oldest one holds the lock, and a client only ever deletes its own. In Redis you have to build the check yourself.

Be clear about what this fixes. A can no longer delete B's lock, so C can't get in while B works. But A and B both still ran the batch: A's lease expired while A was working, and no release script can undo that. The next two sections deal with that.

sim.title: Pod A releases with GET, compare, then DEL
sim.intro: lock = 1 means the key holds A's token, 2 means B's token, 0 means there is no key. A releases the slow way: three steps. Can you make A delete B's lock?

steps.code: GET lock:settle == tok-A? (if not: stop, it isn't mine)
full GC: the JVM stops for 12 s
(10 s later) A's lease ends: Redis deletes the key
SET lock:settle tok-B NX PX 10000 (only if no key)
OK: B holds the lock and starts the batch

goal.say: A deleted B's lock. A's GET saw its own token, then A paused; by the time its DEL arrived, the key held B's token. B is still running the batch and the key is gone, so any pod's SET NX succeeds now. Inside one script, nothing can run between the compare and the delete.

try.title: Release by token, with a script and with DELEX
steps: At a redis-cli prompt (docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli), clear the key, then let pod B take the lock with token tok-b-6f1e.
Play pod A's late release with the script and A's old token, then read the key. Then try DELEX (Redis 8.4) with A's token and with B's.
Take the lock as pod C with a 2-second lease and extend it with SET ... IFEQ. Then try to extend it with A's token.

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
DEL lock:settle
SET lock:settle tok-b-6f1e NX PX 30000
EVAL "if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1]) end return 0" 1 lock:settle tok-a-91c2
GET lock:settle
DELEX lock:settle IFEQ tok-a-91c2
DELEX lock:settle IFEQ tok-b-6f1e
SET lock:settle tok-c-0d77 NX PX 2000
SET lock:settle tok-c-0d77 IFEQ tok-c-0d77 PX 30000
PTTL lock:settle
SET lock:settle tok-a-91c2 IFEQ tok-a-91c2 PX 30000

try.expect: The first DEL prints (integer) 0, or 1 if an earlier run left the key behind. The SET prints OK. The script prints (integer) 0 and GET still shows "tok-b-6f1e": A's late release left B's lock alone. DELEX ... IFEQ tok-a-91c2 prints (integer) 0, and DELEX ... IFEQ tok-b-6f1e prints (integer) 1. C's SET prints OK, the extend prints OK, and PTTL shows (integer) 29999 or close: the 2-second lease is now 30 seconds. Extending with A's token prints (nil) and changes nothing.

sections.h: Renewal narrows the gap, and consensus doesn't close it
sections.html:
How long should the lease be? Too short, and a slow batch outlives it. Too long, and a crashed holder blocks everyone until it ends: with a 10-minute lease, a pod that dies one second in stalls the batch for 9 minutes 59 seconds.

The usual answer is to keep the lease short and renew it while the work runs, as lesson 4's holders did. Redisson, a Java client that builds locks and other objects on top of Redis, does this for you and calls it the watchdog. RLock.lock() with no lease time takes a lease of lockWatchdogTimeout, 30 seconds by default, and keeps extending it while the Redisson client that took it is running. In the demo, with the timeout set to 3 seconds, the lock's TTL stayed between about 2,000 and 3,000 ms for 4 seconds: the watchdog put it back to 3,000 about once a second, a third of the timeout. With an explicit lease, lock.lock(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS), there is no watchdog, and the key was gone after 2 seconds whether or not the work was done. Redisson's lock is a hash whose field is the client's id plus the thread id, so the same thread can take it again, like a ReentrantLock, and only that thread may unlock it.

Renewal narrows the gap and doesn't close it. The watchdog is a thread in the same JVM, so a stop-the-world pause stops it too, and so does every other cause from lesson 4. Checking "do I still hold it?" right before each write doesn't save you either: lesson 4's sweep showed that a second check cuts stale writes about 14 times and leaves the ones whose pause starts after it.

A lock service built on consensus doesn't change that. etcd and ZooKeeper replicate every change to a majority of their nodes before they answer, so a crashed server can't lose a lock the way an asynchronous Redis replica can (section 5, and the Consensus track). But their locks are leases too. An etcd lock key is attached to a lease with a TTL that the client keeps alive, and a ZooKeeper lock is an ephemeral node that disappears when the client's session times out. A paused client stops its keep-alives like any other. Jepsen tested etcd 3.4.3 in 2020. Its key-value operations stayed strict serializable through pauses, crashes, clock skew and partitions, but its locks did not give mutual exclusion, even on a healthy cluster: with lease TTLs of 1 to 3 seconds, two clients held a lock at the same time within minutes. A set guarded by an etcd lock, with 2-second TTLs, five clients and pauses every 5 seconds, lost about 18% of its acknowledged updates. An etcd bug made it worse (a waiting client was granted the lock without a check that its lease was still alive, issue 11456, fixed after 3.4.3), but no server fix can stop a client that pauses after it got the lock. Jepsen's advice was to use etcd locks for performance and to fence every write with the lock key's revision. The next section says what that means.

try.title: Watch Redisson's watchdog renew a lease
steps: Run WatchdogDemo or WatchdogDemoKt from the labs folder. It takes about 8 seconds. The demo sets lockWatchdogTimeout to 3 seconds so the renewals are easy to see.
Read the first PTTL line. What is the lowest value, and how often does it jump back up?
Read the second line, with a fixed 2-second lease. Then run the demo again and compare the two fencing tokens with the first run.

code.title: WatchdogDemo.java
code.html: package sfz.dist.l05.demo; import org.redisson.Redisson; import org.redisson.api.RFencedLock; import org.redisson.api.RLock; import org.redisson.api.RedissonClient; import org.redisson.config.Config; import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** Watch Redisson's lock watchdog renew a lease, then a lock with a fixed lease run out, then fencing tokens. */ public class WatchdogDemo { static final String LOCK = "demo:dist05:lock:settle"; public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Config config = new Config(); config.useSingleServer().setAddress("redis://localhost:6379"); config.setLockWatchdogTimeout(3_000); // the default is 30 s; 3 s keeps the demo short RedissonClient redisson = Redisson.create(config); try (RedisClient redis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build()) { redis.del(LOCK); RLock lock = redisson.getLock(LOCK); lock.lock(); // no lease given: the watchdog keeps it alive System.out.println("lock() with the watchdog. Redis holds a " + redis.type(LOCK) + ": " + redis.hgetAll(LOCK)); StringBuilder ttls = new StringBuilder(); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { Thread.sleep(500); ttls.append(redis.pttl(LOCK)).append(' '); } System.out.println(" PTTL every 500 ms for 4 s: " + ttls.toString().trim()); lock.unlock(); lock.lock(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // a fixed 2 s lease: no watchdog ttls.setLength(0); for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) { Thread.sleep(500); ttls.append(redis.pttl(LOCK)).append(' '); } System.out.println("lock(2, SECONDS), no watchdog."); System.out.println(" PTTL every 500 ms for 3 s: " + ttls.toString().trim() + " (-2: the key is gone)"); System.out.println(" isHeldByCurrentThread() = " + lock.isHeldByCurrentThread()); RFencedLock fenced = redisson.getFencedLock("demo:dist05:fenced:settle"); Long first = fenced.lockAndGetToken(); fenced.unlock(); Long second = fenced.lockAndGetToken(); fenced.unlock(); System.out.println("RFencedLock tokens for two acquisitions: " + first + ", " + second); } finally { redisson.shutdown(); } } }

alt.title: WatchdogDemo.kt
alt.html: package sfz.dist.l05.demo import org.redisson.Redisson import org.redisson.config.Config import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** Watch Redisson's lock watchdog renew a lease, then a lock with a fixed lease run out, then fencing tokens. */ private const val LOCK = "demo:dist05:lock:settle" fun main() { val config = Config().apply { useSingleServer().setAddress("redis://localhost:6379") setLockWatchdogTimeout(3_000) // the default is 30 s; 3 s keeps the demo short } val redisson = Redisson.create(config) try { RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build().use { redis -> redis.del(LOCK) val lock = redisson.getLock(LOCK) fun pttlEvery500ms(times: Int) = (1..times).joinToString(" ") { Thread.sleep(500); redis.pttl(LOCK).toString() } lock.lock() // no lease given: the watchdog keeps it alive println("lock() with the watchdog. Redis holds a ${redis.type(LOCK)}: ${redis.hgetAll(LOCK)}") println(" PTTL every 500 ms for 4 s: ${pttlEvery500ms(8)}") lock.unlock() lock.lock(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // a fixed 2 s lease: no watchdog val ttls = pttlEvery500ms(6) println("lock(2, SECONDS), no watchdog.") println(" PTTL every 500 ms for 3 s: $ttls (-2: the key is gone)") println(" isHeldByCurrentThread() = ${lock.isHeldByCurrentThread}") val fenced = redisson.getFencedLock("demo:dist05:fenced:settle") val first = fenced.lockAndGetToken().also { fenced.unlock() } val second = fenced.lockAndGetToken().also { fenced.unlock() } println("RFencedLock tokens for two acquisitions: $first, $second") } } finally { redisson.shutdown() } }

try.expect: The first line shows a hash such as {7aadc447-...:3=1}: the field is the Redisson client id and the thread id, the value a hold count of 1. The PTTL readings saw-tooth, for example 2418 2954 2432 2955 2451 2957 2451 2956: they never fall far below 2,000 ms because the watchdog resets the lease to 3,000 about every second. With lock(2, SECONDS) they count down, 1494 987 484 -2 -2 -2: no renewals, the key is gone after 2 seconds, and isHeldByCurrentThread() is false. The fencing tokens are 1, 2 on the first run and 3, 4 on the next: the counter lives in Redis and keeps growing.

refs.title: How to do distributed locking (Martin Kleppmann)

sections.h: Fencing tokens let the resource refuse a stale holder
sections.html:
If the holder can't know that its lease ended, someone else has to refuse its late writes. The only party that sees every write is the resource itself: the payout file store, the ledger table, the bank's API.

That takes one more number. Each time a client acquires the lock, it also gets a fencing token, a number that grows with every acquisition: 33 for A, 34 for B. Every write to the resource carries the token. The resource remembers the highest token it has accepted and refuses any write with a lower one. When A wakes from its pause and writes with 33 after B has written with 34, the write is refused. The stepper plays it with the numbers from Kleppmann's post. Lesson 4's ledger was one comparison away from this: its lease ids grew with every grant, and the writes that clobbered a newer holder's update were exactly the ones carrying a smaller id.

In Redis the counter is INCR fence:{settle}, run by the same script that takes the lock, so a token is issued exactly when a lock is: if SET ... NX PX succeeds, return INCR, otherwise return 0. The lab's RedisLock does that. Consensus systems already have such a number. Every change to etcd gets the next value of one cluster-wide revision, and the revision at which a client's lock key was created works as its token. Every change to ZooKeeper gets a zxid, a transaction id that only grows. Raft's term and Kafka's producer epoch are the same idea, and the Consensus and Messaging tracks come back to them.

The resource side is the half people miss, because it isn't lock code at all. In Oracle it is UPDATE payout_files SET content = :c, fence = :t WHERE batch = :b AND fence <= :t, and zero rows updated means "you are a stale holder". The lab's PayoutLedger models that store.

A Redis counter needs two kinds of care. It must never go backwards, so it gets no TTL, and it must live on a Redis whose eviction policy can't drop it (the Caching track's lesson on expiry and eviction: the volatile-* policies only evict keys that have a TTL). And it is only as durable as that server. If a failover loses its last increments, because replication is asynchronous (the Caching track's lesson on persistence and replication), a new holder can get a number that was already handed out. Kleppmann argues that this is why fencing tokens belong to a consensus system such as etcd or ZooKeeper.

His split is the first question to ask about any lock. Is it for efficiency, so that two pods don't do the same work twice, and a rare double run only costs some CPU or a duplicate email? Or is it for correctness, where a double run pays merchants twice? An efficiency lock can be a single Redis key with a token, like the Caching track's stampede lock. A correctness lock needs the resource to check something: fencing tokens, or a design where the second run fails anyway, such as a unique constraint on the batch id in the payouts table.

stepper.title: Fencing tokens: the store refuses the paused holder
stepper.intro: Tokens 33 and 34, as in Kleppmann's example. The store stands in for your database.

frames.say: The GC ends. A carries on from where it stopped and writes its version of the file with fence 33. No check in A would have caught this: the pause could have come after any check. The store sees 33, below the 34 it already accepted, and refuses. B's file stays.

frames.say: Take the check away and A's write lands after B's: the file the bank receives is A's stale version, built before B's run, missing 12 merchants. The lock kept A and B apart only while A's lease was alive. The token keeps them apart at the one place that sees every write. That is why fencing needs the resource to cooperate: in Oracle, an UPDATE ... WHERE fence <= :token.

try.title: Fence a write by hand
steps: At a redis-cli prompt (docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli), clear the store's hash, set the fence counter to 32 and take two tokens, one for pod A and one for pod B.
A Redis hash plays the payout store here, and the script plays its rule: refuse a fence lower than the one stored. Let B write with its token first, then A with its older one.
Read the stored file. Then, before you run it, predict what A's write would return if B had never written.

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
DEL payout:batch-118
SET fence:{settle} 32
INCR fence:{settle}
INCR fence:{settle}
EVAL "local f = tonumber(redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 'fence') or '0') if tonumber(ARGV[1]) < f then return 0 end redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'fence', ARGV[1], 'content', ARGV[2]) return 1" 1 payout:batch-118 34 "B: 4210 payouts"
EVAL "local f = tonumber(redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 'fence') or '0') if tonumber(ARGV[1]) < f then return 0 end redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'fence', ARGV[1], 'content', ARGV[2]) return 1" 1 payout:batch-118 33 "A: 4198 payouts"
HGETALL payout:batch-118

try.expect: The first DEL prints (integer) 0, or 1 if an earlier run left the key behind. The two INCRs print (integer) 33 (A's token) and (integer) 34 (B's). B's write returns (integer) 1, and A's returns (integer) 0: 33 is lower than the stored 34. HGETALL shows fence "34" and content "B: 4210 payouts". Had B never written, A's write would return 1: fencing only refuses a holder once a newer one has written, which is exactly the case that matters.

refs.title: Distributed locks: disclaimer about consistency (Redis docs)

sections.h: Redlock, and the argument about it
sections.html:
Everything so far in Redis used one server, and one server can fail. Adding a replica doesn't make the lock safe, because replication is asynchronous. Pod A takes the lock on the primary, the primary crashes before the write reaches the replica, the replica is promoted without the key, and pod B takes the same lock. The Redis docs give this exact sequence.

Redlock is Redis's answer. Run N independent Redis masters, usually 5, with no replication between them. To acquire, a client sends SET key token NX PX ttl to all 5 in parallel, with a short timeout for each, and holds the lock only if it got a majority (at least 3) and the whole attempt took less than the TTL. What is left of the TTL after the attempt is how long it may hold the lock. If it fails, it releases on all 5.

In 2016 Martin Kleppmann argued that Redlock is unsafe when correctness depends on it. Its safety depends on timing: bounded network delay, bounded pauses, and clocks that don't jump. If one node's clock jumps forward, its key expires early and two clients can each get a majority. A GC pause while the replies are on their way leaves a client believing it holds a lock that has already expired. And Redlock has no fencing tokens, because a random value has no order. His advice: for efficiency, a single Redis is enough; for correctness, use a consensus system and fencing.

Salvatore Sanfilippo (antirez), who designed Redlock, replied within days. He argued that Redlock needs clocks that tick at about the same rate, not synchronized ones, and that clock jumps come from administrators and badly configured NTP, which you can avoid. He argued that a pause before the client's final time check is caught by that check, and a pause after it hurts every lease-based lock equally. And he argued that the large random token can be used for check-and-set on the resource instead of a counter. He agreed that Redis should use a monotonic clock for expiry.

Both have a point, and the practical answer has settled. The Redis docs now ask you to read both posts, recommend fencing tokens when correctness matters, and warn that Redis doesn't use a monotonic clock for TTLs. Redisson deprecated its RedLock object in favor of RLock and RFencedLock, saying the algorithm's safety guarantees are contested. So: use a single Redis lock with a token for efficiency. For correctness, make the resource enforce it with fencing tokens it checks, a unique constraint, or a lock in the database itself, such as Oracle's SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the batch row. Five Redis servers cost more than either option and settle neither argument.

refs.title: How to do distributed locking (Martin Kleppmann)

analogy: A Redis lock is a hotel key card with a checkout time. The front desk (Redis) gives one guest a card for room 118 that works until 11:00, and won't issue another while it is valid. At 11:00 it hands a new card to the next guest. The front desk keeps its side of the deal perfectly, but it never walks up to the room: if the first guest is still inside, napping past checkout (a GC pause), both guests now think the room is theirs. A fencing token is a number printed on each card, with a door that remembers the highest number it has seen and refuses lower ones. Card 34 opens the door, so card 33 never will again. The analogy breaks on who checks: a hotel door is consulted every time someone enters, while a Redis lock is consulted once, when you take it, and the resource never asks again unless you make it check the token.
world: Before you take a Redis lock, look for a tool that already makes the work run once. Temporal allows only one running workflow per workflow id, so a settlement workflow with the id settle-batch-118 can't run twice at once, and that check doesn't depend on anyone's clock. In Oracle, a unique constraint on the batch id in the payouts table makes a second run fail at the insert, and SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the batch row is a lock that lives with the data. A Kafka consumer group already gives each partition to one consumer. Use a Redis lock for efficiency jobs where a rare double run is harmless: refreshing a cache, recomputing a report, the Caching track's stampede lock. When you do use it for something that moves money, pass the fencing token down to the write, as a column the update checks.
mistake: The most common mistake is a lock that is only correct while nothing is slow: SET lock NX PX 30000 to take it, DEL lock in a finally block, and a critical section that writes to the database with no other check. It passes every test, because tests don't pause for 35 seconds, and moving it to etcd or ZooKeeper doesn't change that. In production a long GC, a slow query or a node under memory pressure lets the lease expire mid-work, a second pod starts, and the first pod's DEL then removes the second pod's lock, letting a third in. People write it this way because it reads like a ReentrantLock, which can't expire behind your back. The fix has three parts: a random token per acquire, release with compare-and-delete (DELEX key IFEQ token on 8.4+, a Lua script before that), and, if a double run costs money, a fencing token or constraint that the resource itself checks.

compare.title: Take the lock, write with the fence, release: Java and Kotlin

java.title: SettlementJob.java
java.html: void settle(String batchId) { Optional<RedisLock.Lease> lease = lock.tryAcquire("settle", Duration.ofSeconds(30)); if (lease.isEmpty()) return; // another pod is running the batch try { String file = buildPayoutFile(batchId); boolean written = ledger.write(batchId, lease.get().fence(), file); // the store checks the fence if (!written) log.warn("lost the lock to a newer holder; file not written"); } finally { lock.release(lease.get()); // compare-and-delete: never another pod's lock } }

kotlin.title: SettlementJob.kt
kotlin.html: inline fun <T> RedisLock.withLock(resource: String, lease: Duration, block: (RedisLock.Lease) -> T): T? { val held = tryAcquire(resource, lease).orElse(null) ?: return null // another pod is running it try { return block(held) } finally { release(held) // compare-and-delete: never another pod's lock } } fun settle(batchId: String) { lock.withLock("settle", Duration.ofSeconds(30)) { lease -> val written = ledger.write(batchId, lease.fence(), buildPayoutFile(batchId)) // the store checks the fence if (!written) log.warn("lost the lock to a newer holder; file not written") } }

compare.note: Both send the same two scripts to Redis: acquire (SET NX PX, then INCR the fence) and compare-and-delete release. Java repeats the try/finally at every call site. Kotlin writes it once as an inline extension function: the lambda's body is copied into the caller, so a return inside it returns from settle, and a caller can't forget the release. Neither version relies on the lock alone. The release in finally can't undo a write made after the lease ran out, so the write carries the fence and the store decides. When write returns false, the pod lost the lock while working and must not report the batch as done.

worked.title: Build the lock one failure at a time

steps.say: First one wins: NX creates the key only if it doesn't exist, and one thread runs each command, so exactly one pod gets OK and the others get nil. It fails the first time a holder crashes: the key never goes away.
Add a deadline inside the same command, and a random token so the holder can prove later that the lock is still its own. A UUID per acquire, never the pod name.
steps.code: String token = UUID.randomUUID().toString(); boolean got = redis.set("lock:settle", token, SetParams.setParams().nx().px(30_000)) != null; // "OK" or null

alt.html: val token = UUID.randomUUID().toString() val got = redis.set("lock:settle", token, SetParams.setParams().nx().px(30_000)) != null // "OK" or null

steps.say: Release only your own lock, compare and delete in one command. On Redis 8.4+ that is DELEX; before that, the three-line Lua script with GET, compare and DEL.
steps.code: boolean released = redis.delex("lock:settle", CompareCondition.valueEq(token)) == 1; // DELEX ... IFEQ token

alt.html: val released = redis.delex("lock:settle", CompareCondition.valueEq(token)) == 1L // DELEX ... IFEQ token

steps.say: Number the holders. The acquire becomes a script that increments a counter only when the SET succeeded, so every holder gets a larger fence than the one before, and a failed attempt uses up nothing.
steps.code:
if redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], ARGV[1], 'NX', 'PX', ARGV[2]) then
    return redis.call('INCR', KEYS[2])     -- KEYS[2] = fence:{settle}, no TTL, ever
end
return 0

steps.say: Make the resource check the number. This is the step that protects the data, and it lives in your database, not in Redis: the update succeeds only for a fence at least as large as the last one written.
steps.code: UPDATE payout_files SET content = :content, fence = :fence WHERE batch = :batch AND fence <= :fence; -- 0 rows: a newer holder already wrote; stop

lab.title: A Redis lock with tokens and fencing, and the store that enforces it
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. All 13 fail: nine in RedisLockTest use the shared Redis container, and four in PayoutLedgerTest need no Docker. Lease expiry in the tests is real but short (200 ms leases), so a few of them take a fraction of a second.

In RedisLock.java, write the ACQUIRE script and tryAcquire. Run ./gradlew :redis:test --tests 'sfz.dist.l05.RedisLockTest'. Most tests pass now. a late release does not delete the next holder's lock still fails: that is the bug in the stub's release.
Fix release with the RELEASE script, and write extend with one SET ... IFEQ.

In PayoutLedger.kt, write write with one compute. Run all 13. The last test in RedisLockTest is the stepper end to end: A's lease expires during a pause, B writes with a larger fence, and A's late write is refused.
hints: if redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], ARGV[1], 'NX', 'PX', ARGV[2]) then return redis.call('INCR', KEYS[2]) end return 0. The Lua number reaches Java as a Long.
redis.set(key, token, SetParams.setParams().condition(CompareCondition.valueEq(token)).px(ms)) returns null when the condition was false, so return reply != null;.
Inside compute, return old to keep the stored file, or PayoutFile(fence, content) to replace it. A var written = false outside the lambda records which branch ran.

drill.title: Safe release from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write release(key, token) with Jedis twice: with the compare-and-delete Lua script, and with the Redis 8.4 command. Then write one sentence on why it can't be a GET in Java followed by a DEL.

answer.html: static final String RELEASE = """ if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1]) end return 0 """; boolean release(String key, String token) { return Long.valueOf(1).equals(redis.eval(RELEASE, List.of(key), List.of(token))); // compare and delete, one command } boolean releaseOnRedis84(String key, String token) { return redis.delex(key, CompareCondition.valueEq(token)) == 1; // DELEX key IFEQ token } // GET then DEL is two commands: a pause between them lets the lease expire, and the DEL removes the next holder's lock

alt.html: val RELEASE = """ if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1]) end return 0 """.trimIndent() fun release(key: String, token: String): Boolean = redis.eval(RELEASE, listOf(key), listOf(token)) == 1L // compare and delete, one command fun releaseOnRedis84(key: String, token: String): Boolean = redis.delex(key, CompareCondition.valueEq(token)) == 1L // DELEX key IFEQ token // GET then DEL is two commands: a pause between them lets the lease expire, and the DEL removes the next holder's lock

recap: A lease is a lock with a deadline in every lock service: SET key token NX PX ttl in Redis, a TTL lease in etcd, a session in ZooKeeper. The service enforces the deadline; nothing makes the holder stop when it passes.
Release with compare-and-delete, a Lua script or DELEX key IFEQ token on Redis 8.4+. Plain DEL, or GET then DEL, can delete the next holder's lock.

Renewing the lease (Redisson's watchdog, 30-second default) covers slow work, not a paused holder. Consensus doesn't help either: Jepsen lost about 18% of the updates guarded by etcd 3.4.3 locks with 2-second leases and pauses.

A fencing token grows with every acquisition and travels with every write, and the resource refuses tokens lower than the highest it has seen. It can be a Redis INCR, etcd's revision or ZooKeeper's zxid.
Redlock takes a majority of 5 independent masters, and its safety for correctness is disputed. Use one Redis lock for efficiency, and fencing or the database for correctness.

explain.prompt: Your settlement job takes a Redis lock with a 30-second lease and releases it with compare-and-delete. A reviewer asks: "What if the job pauses for 40 seconds?" Explain what happens and what you would change.
explain.answer: Redis deletes the lock after 30 seconds, as it should, and nothing tells our job. A second pod's SET NX succeeds and it starts the same batch, while ours is frozen in a GC pause or cut off by the network. When ours wakes up it carries on and writes its payout file, so two pods have written. The compare-and-delete stops us from deleting the second pod's lock, but it can't stop our write, and checking the lock before writing doesn't help, because the pause can fall between the check and the write. A watchdog that renews the lease covers slow work but stops during a pause like everything else, and moving the lock to etcd or ZooKeeper wouldn't change that: their locks are leases too. So the protection has to sit at the resource. I'd have the acquire script also INCR a fence counter and pass that number to the write, and make the payouts table accept a write only when the fence is at least the last one stored: UPDATE ... WHERE fence <= :fence. Zero rows updated tells the job it lost the lock. Since this lock is about not paying merchants twice, I'd also add a unique constraint on the batch id, so a second payout file can't be inserted at all.

deeper.html:
Chubby's sequencers. Google's Chubby lock service had fencing from the start. A holder asks for a sequencer, an opaque string that names the lock and its generation, and passes it to every server it writes to; the server checks it with Chubby or against the newest sequencer it has seen. For servers that can't check, Chubby keeps a lock released by a failed holder unavailable for a lock-delay of up to a minute. That narrows the window for a late write without closing it, which is the whole story of lesson 4 in one setting.

Locks inside the database. If the resource is a database, its own locks avoid the two-system problem entirely. Oracle's SELECT ... FOR UPDATE holds a row lock until the transaction ends, and a session that dies releases it with its transaction. Oracle's DBMS_LOCK and PostgreSQL's advisory locks (pg_advisory_lock) give named locks that also end with the session. The lock belongs to the same session as the data changes. If the client pauses, the row stays locked and every other session waits; if its connection dies, the database rolls its transaction back and frees the lock. At no moment do two clients both hold it, and no clock decides when it ends.

Redisson's fenced lock. RFencedLock (redisson.getFencedLock(name), then lockAndGetToken() or tryLockAndGetToken(...)) returns a token that grows with every acquisition, like the lab's RedisLock. Redisson's docs say the guarded service should accept a token only if it is at least as large as the previous one, the same rule as the lab's PayoutLedger.

Waiting for a lock. The lab's tryAcquire tries once. A loop that retries at a fixed interval makes every waiting pod hit Redis at the same moment; retry after a random delay instead, as the Redis docs recommend for Redlock. Redisson's tryLock(wait, lease, unit) subscribes to an unlock notification over Redis pub/sub, which the Messaging track covers, instead of polling. etcd and ZooKeeper clients wait with a watch on the key just ahead of their own.

Clocks. Redis computes TTLs from the wall clock, not a monotonic one, so a server whose clock jumps forward expires leases early. The Redis docs mention this in their consistency disclaimer, and it is one more reason, after lesson 3, to run NTP in slewing mode on lock servers rather than letting it step the clock.
